newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's ruling party wins peaceful state vote.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's ruling party wins peaceful state vote.

text.p: Early election results on Monday dealt Mexico's ruling party a double blow in the troubled state of Guerrero, where more than half of the voters stayed home and two big towns appeared likely to fall to the opposition for the first time ever.

Sunday's vote for 76 mayors and 28 local deputies in one of Mexico's most violent states passed off peacefully. Marxist guerrillas kept their promise of a cease-fire and troops persuing them stayed confined to barracks.

Final results were not expected until mid-week but partial returns showed the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) winning Iguala, the state's third biggest town, and running close behind the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) in the tourist resort of Acapulco, Guerrero's biggest and richest city.
The conservative National Action Party (PAN) was ahead in the colonial silver town of Taxco and elsewhere the PRI appeared likely to keep most of its 68 mayors in the state.

Fears of trouble and heavy rain in some areas may have kept many voters at home. Local PRI officials estimated half of registered voters stayed away, but independent electoral observers said the figure was nearer to 60 percent.
Acting Gov. Angel Aguirre nevertheless called the elections an unprecedented step for democracy in Guerrero, a state plagued by post-electoral violence in the past.

The PRI, which has ruled Mexico for 67 years, showed the resilience of its political machinery, leading in 50 of 60 town hall races counted so far and in 24 of 26 state congressional contests. In the town of Quechultenango, it won 2,513 out of 2,578 votes cast.

Sunday's largely peaceful vote helped ease tensions that have been building after a year of rising political violence between the government and increasingly angry PRD supporters. About 120 people, mostly leftwingers, have died in political violence over the past year.

Election analysts said while the vote was probably the cleanest yet, President Ernesto Zedillo's promises of totally fair elections had not come entirely true. Electoral watchdog Alianza Civica, a private group, said there were a host of problems including opposition figures whose names were left off voter lists, vote-buying and intimidation of voters by the ruling PRI.

"Throughout the state we noted that practices were continuing which we would rather were not continued, such as the buying of votes and the missing-off of names," Alianza Civica National Committee member Jose Luis Baracas said.

A Reuter correspondent who witnessed voting in different parts of the state on Sunday said voters and officials repeatedly alleged PRI activists had promised voters money or bags of cement in return for their support.

PRD leader Manuel Lopez Obrador appeared pleased with the vote late on Sunday and claimed that his party -- the second biggest force in the state prior to Sunday's election with six town halls -- had made big gains against the PRI.
Lopez Obrador said the vote had been peaceful but that he would wait until final returns came in to say whether the party would contest any of the results.

All sides praised the Mexican army for returning to their barracks during the election, following an earlier cease-fire by rebels of the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), a guerrilla group that sprang up this summer in Guerrero and launched attacks on several army and police posts in the state.
